author: Cyril of Alexandria
occasion: Cyril writes to Photius, a presbyter of Alexandria, presenting a conditional argument about the consequences of blending two natures into one mixture.
argument: The surviving text consists of a single conditional statement. Cyril argues that if two natures, being of different substances, are blended into one mixture, then neither nature is preserved. Instead, both are confused together and destroyed. The text presents this as a logical consequence of a hypothetical position, without naming opponents or explicitly identifying a Christological error.

outline.move: Cyril presents a conditional argument: if two natures of different substances are blended into one mixture, neither is preserved but both are confused and destroyed.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Cyril writes to Photius, a presbyter of Alexandria, presenting a conditional argument about the consequences of blending two natures into one mixture.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source only contains a heading and one conditional sentence; there is no evidence of Cyril 'writing to' Photius in any epistolary frame beyond the title, and no epistolary opening or closing survives.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The text presents this as a logical consequence of a hypothetical position, without naming opponents or explicitly identifying a Christological error.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Εἰ δὲ κέκρανται αἱ δύο φύσεις εἰς μῖξιν μίαν, ἑτεροούσιοι τυγχάνουσαι, οὐδ' ὁποτέρα σώζεται, ἀλλ' ἀμφότεραι συγχυθεῖσαι ἠφανίσθησαν
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source does not indicate whether this is 'presented as a logical consequence of a hypothetical position' or stated as Cyril's own view; the conditional form (εἰ) is present but its rhetorical function cannot be determined from the fragment.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Cyril presents a conditional argument: if two natures of different substances are blended into one mixture, neither is preserved but both are confused and destroyed.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The participial phrase 'being of different substances' modifies 'two natures' as a factual characterization in the conditional, not as part of the protasis condition itself; the outline should not treat this as a premise within the 'if' clause.

_unresolved_facts.claim: A presbyter of Alexandria to whom Cyril addresses this letter.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The genitive Ἀλεξανδρείας likely modifies πρεσβύτερον (presbyter of Alexandria), not Φώτιον; Photius's see is not specified, and 'of Alexandria' may describe the presbyter's office, not his residence or Photius himself.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The text is presented as Cyril's letter to Photius; the surviving sentence is Cyril's own statement.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The attribution 'Τοῦ αὐτοῦ' (of the same [author]) indicates this is a collection heading, not a voice marker; we cannot determine if the conditional is Cyril's own view, a quotation, or a dialectical move.
